concepts.name: Radian measure
concepts.learningObjective: The student can locate an angle in radians on the unit circle and convert between degrees and radians.
concepts.primer: Angles measured by arc length on the unit circle; one full turn is 2π.
keyFacts: π radians is half a revolution, or 180°.
pitfalls: π radians is half a circle; a full circle is 2π.

concepts.name: Period of sin(bx) and cos(bx)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can compute the period of y = sin(bx) or cos(bx) and explain why a larger b shortens it.
concepts.primer: The horizontal length of one full cycle, 2π/|b|.
keyFacts: The period of y = sin(bx) is 2π/|b|.
Increasing b makes the graph repeat more often.
pitfalls: A bigger b squeezes the wave, so sin(2x) has period π.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.learningObjective: The student can read the amplitude from an equation or graph and distinguish it from the peak-to-trough distance.
concepts.primer: |A| in y = A·sin(x): the height of the wave above its midline.
keyFacts: The amplitude of y = A sin x is |A|.
Changing A does not change the period.
pitfalls: Peak-to-trough is twice the amplitude; amplitude is |A|.

concepts.name: Solving sin(x) = k on [0, 2π)
concepts.learningObjective: The student can find every solution of a basic sine equation on one period.
concepts.primer: Isolate the sine, find the reference angle, then use the quadrants where sine has that sign.
keyFacts: Sine is positive in quadrants I and II.
pitfalls: It has two: π/6 in quadrant I and 5π/6 in quadrant II.

title: The Resonance Circuit

theme.setting: The observatory's brass circuit board, where every conduit carries a sine wave

premise: The observatory's orrery has gone dark. Its circuit board carries resonance from the source crystal to the core, but the conduits are twisted and five seals block the way. Route the wave and break every seal by reading its rhythm.

characters.name: Cog
characters.role: brass owl who whistles when a conduit connects

characters.name: The Core
characters.role: the orrery's heart, sealed until the circuit is whole

encounters.targetMisconception: π radians is a full circle.
encounters.prompt: The altar's rune line runs from 0 to 2π. Step onto 5π/6.
hints: A full turn is 2π, so π sits exactly halfway along the line.
5π/6 is a little less than π. Count in sixths of π.
It sits between π/2 and π, closer to the right one.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Radians measure distance around the circle: π is half a turn, so fractions of π land proportionally along the line.
encounters.debriefLine: The rune line was the unit circle unrolled: 5π/6 is 5/12 of a full turn.

sourceRef.quote: An angle of π radians corresponds to half a revolution.

encounters.targetMisconception: sin(2x) has period 4π, twice as long as sin(x).
encounters.prompt: The vault door's rings spin on y = sin(2t). Set the dial to one full period so the rings lock.
hints: A period is how long the rings take to come back to where they started.
For y = sin(b·t), one period lasts 2π/|b|.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Doubling b doesn't double the period, it halves it: the rings spin faster, so each cycle is shorter.
encounters.debriefLine: The door followed y = sin(2t); its period is π, because 2π/|b| with b = 2.

sourceRef.quote: The period of y = sin(bx) is 2π/|b|.

encounters.targetMisconception: Amplitude is the distance from peak to trough.
encounters.prompt: Four conduits hum on four different waves. Link each wave to how far it swings from its midline.

pairs.why: The minus sign flips the wave; the swing is |−2| = 2.
The 4 changes the period, not the swing.
Adding 4 moves the midline up; the swing is still 1.

hints: Amplitude is measured from the midline, not from peak to trough.
Only the number multiplying sin or cos sets the swing; take its absolute value.
Ignore the number inside the brackets and anything added on the end.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Check what each number does: the multiplier sets the swing, the number inside sets the speed, and a number added on the end only moves the midline.
encounters.debriefLine: Amplitude is |A|: you linked 4 waves to their swing, ignoring period changes and midline shifts.

sourceRef.quote: The amplitude of y = A sin x is |A|.

encounters.targetMisconception: sin(x) = 1/2 has only one solution on [0, 2π).
encounters.prompt: The glyph door opens only if its planks show how to solve 2sin(x) = 1 on [0, 2π). One plank doesn't belong.

steps: Sine is positive in quadrants I and II
Write both solutions: x = π/6 and x = 5π/6
decoys: Take the inverse sine of 2 first

hints: Get the sine by itself before anything else.
Which angle in quadrant I has a sine of 1/2?
Sine is positive in two quadrants, which is why there are two answers.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Order matters: you can't find the angle until the sine is alone.
encounters.debriefLine: You solved 2sin(x) = 1 in 4 moves: isolate, reference angle, quadrants, both solutions.

sourceRef.quote: To solve a trigonometric equation, first isolate the trigonometric function.

encounters.targetMisconception: sin(2x) has period 4π, twice as long as sin(x).
encounters.prompt: The apprentice at the gate is stuck: why does a bigger b in y = sin(bx) make the period shorter? Explain it in your own words.

params.listener: the gate's apprentice, who only memorised the formula
params.question: Why does a bigger b in y = sin(bx) make the period shorter?

ideas.label: the angle one wave needs
ideas.followUp: But what has to happen inside the sine before the wave starts repeating?
ideas.exemplar: One full cycle of the wave happens when bx runs through 2π.

ideas.label: how quickly the inside grows
ideas.followUp: Okay, and what does a larger b do to the way bx changes as x moves along?
ideas.exemplar: A bigger b makes bx grow faster, so x reaches that point sooner.

ideas.label: the formula for the period
ideas.followUp: Can you turn that into a formula for the period in terms of b?
ideas.exemplar: That is why the period equals 2π/b, and dividing by a bigger number gives a shorter period.

misconceptions.correction: Wait, try b = 1 and then b = 2. Which one finishes its wave first?

hints: Start from what one complete wave of sin means for the angle inside it.
Think of bx as a clock: with a bigger b, how fast does the clock run as x increases?
Say that one cycle is when bx covers 2π, a bigger b gets there faster, so the period is 2π/b.
encounters.wrongFeedback: Your apprentice is still confused. Think about the angle inside sin and how fast it grows.
encounters.debriefLine: Period = 2π/b: a bigger b makes the angle bx sweep through 2π faster, so each wave is shorter. Model answer: One full cycle of the wave happens when bx runs through 2π. A bigger b makes bx grow faster, so x reaches that point sooner. That is why the period equals 2π/b, and dividing by a bigger number gives a shorter period.

solution.exemplar: One full cycle of the wave happens when bx runs through 2π. A bigger b makes bx grow faster, so x reaches that point sooner. That is why the period equals 2π/b, and dividing by a bigger number gives a shorter period.

encounters.prompt: The Warden's shield spins on y = 3sin((π/2)t). Match its period to break through, and don't let the big swing fool you.
hints: The 3 in front sets how far the shield swings, not how fast.
Divide 2π by π/2: the π's cancel.
encounters.wrongFeedback: The amplitude doesn't change the timing. Only b does.
encounters.debriefLine: The Warden's shield followed y = 3sin((π/2)t): amplitude 3 (how far), period 4 (how fast).

sourceRef.quote: The value of A stretches the graph vertically but leaves the period unchanged.

intro.text: The board is dead cold. Twist the conduits so the wave can flow, and when it touches a seal, crack it.

outro.text: Hear that hum? The whole circuit resonates. The orrery turns again.

beats.text: This seal pulses on a sine wave. Watch how fast, not how far.
Only a true period reaches my core.
Resonance accepted. The circuit is whole.
